title: Shop SDK lead capture now supports Rich Authorization Requests
summary:
You can now request the specific profile data your app needs during Shop SDK lead capture, including details that aren't saved on the user's Shop profile. Use Rich Authorization Requests (RAR) to select which fields are required and which ones users can skip. Existing integrations don't need changes to continue working; RAR is opt-in.

What changed

Lead capture now accepts an authorizationDetails attribute. The attribute takes a serialized JSON array that lists the fields your app needs and marks each one as required or optional. For example, this request requires a phone number and makes birthdate optional:

const authorizationDetails = JSON.stringify([
  {
    type: 'urn:shopify:shop_app:data-sharing:v1',
    datatypes: [
      {name: 'phone_number', required: true},
      {name: 'birthdate', required: false},
    ],
  },
]);

You can request given name, family name, phone number, and birthdate with RAR. The existing OAuth scopes shop_app:user:profile and shop_app:user:phone let you request existing names and phone numbers, respectively, but don't prompt users to provide missing values.

Before a user authorizes your app, Shop asks them for any requested fields that they haven't shared with your app. Users must provide values for required fields and can skip optional ones. If a user declines to authorize your app, then onComplete doesn't include a shopConsentToken, even if the user signs in to the store. Handle a missing shopConsentToken as an expected outcome.

Who's affected

This change applies to apps that use Shop SDK lead capture. To read data that you request with RAR, your app needs a client secret and a trusted server.

As with existing lead capture, an authorized phone number returned by Shop can replace a different phone number on the store's customer record. Existing names aren't replaced.

What to do

To request data with RAR:

  1. Pass your serialized array as attributes.authorizationDetails when you create the lead capture instance. To also request the user's identifier and email, set attributes.scope to 'shop_app:oauth', as shown in the guide.
  2. In onComplete, send shopConsentToken to your server when the event includes one. The event doesn't include the requested data. If the event includes customerUpdateErrors, then the update to the store's customer record failed.
  3. From your server, exchange the consent token with the fetchTokensForUser mutation on the Shop Partners API. Read the authorized fields from the response or from the Shop Users API, and handle null for fields that weren't granted or have no value.
  4. Before you ship, test a completed authorization, a skipped optional field, a declined authorization, and a request with malformed authorizationDetails JSON that returns invalid_authorization_details in onError. For the request format and error handling, see the lead capture guide.

title: Start Sidekick conversations from your app
summary:
Embedded apps can now launch Sidekick with a pre-filled prompt using the Sidekick Launch API, so merchants can get contextual help without leaving your app.

From within the Shopify admin, your app can start a Sidekick conversation on the merchant’s behalf. For example, add an Ask Sidekick button next to a report that calls shopify.sidekick.launch({ message }). Sidekick opens with your prompt sent as the merchant’s message.

Learn more in the Sidekick Launch API documentation.

title: Shopify App Pricing: Plan Feature Targeting
summary:
You can now add store requirements to public plans in Shopify App Pricing. A merchant whose store does not have a required feature cannot subscribe to that plan. Store requirements are optional, so no action is required.

What changed

The plan editor in the Partner Dashboard has a new Store requirements section for public plans. You can select one or both of these requirements:

  • Checkout UI extensions (all pages) and branding customizations: The store can use app customizations on every step of checkout.
  • Direct company catalogs (B2B): The store can assign catalogs directly to its B2B customers.

Shopify checks the requirements on the plan selection page and again when the merchant approves the charge. On the plan selection page, the select button is unavailable on plans that the store does not qualify for.

Who's affected

Store requirements are available only on public plans in Shopify App Pricing. They are not available on private plans or on charges that you create with the Billing API. Requirements do not change existing subscriptions:

  • A merchant with an active subscription keeps the plan when you add or change its requirements.
  • If that subscription is cancelled, then the merchant must meet the current requirements to resume that plan.

Visitors who are not logged in to the Shopify App Store continue to see all of your public plans.

Why this matters

Before this change, a merchant could subscribe to a plan that depended on a feature their store did not have. Store requirements stop that subscription before the merchant pays for functionality that cannot work in their store.

What to do

No action is required. Add a store requirement only when a plan cannot work without the feature. Every store without the feature is blocked from the plan.

To add a store requirement:

  1. Open the plan editor for a public plan. For the full steps, refer to public plans.
  2. Under Store requirements, select the features that the plan needs.
  3. Click Save.
  4. Open your plan selection page from a store that does not have the feature.

The select button on that plan is unavailable, and the message names the missing feature. A store that has the feature can still select the plan.

  • Shopify App Pricing

title: Shopify App Store: Estimated local-currency prices
summary:
Merchants who are billed in a currency other than USD now see estimated prices for your app in their billing currency. No action is required on your part, and you can continue to set prices in USD.

What changed

The Shopify App Store and the Shopify admin show app prices as estimates in the merchant's billing currency, for example €17.67 EUR/month. Estimates appear in these places:

  • Your app listing and app cards on the Shopify App Store.
  • The plan selection page, the charge approval page, and app billing details in the Shopify admin.

A disclaimer next to each estimate shows the exchange rate. The disclaimer links to local currency billing in the Shopify Help Center.

Previously, these merchants saw USD prices and the message "All charges are billed in USD." Shopify still converts each charge to the merchant's billing currency when it issues the charge.

Who's affected

This change applies to apps that set prices in USD, with Shopify App Pricing or with the Billing API. Merchants see estimates when their billing currency is one of these 14 currencies: AUD, CAD, CHF, CZK, DKK, EUR, GBP, INR, JPY, NOK, PLN, RON, SEK, and SGD.

These cases do not change:

  • Merchants who are billed in USD see USD prices.
  • Charges that you create in another supported currency with the Billing API show their own amount.
  • Prices on app pages that you control are not converted.

What to do

No action is required. Your prices and earnings do not change. If your support content shows plan prices or screenshots, then check that it matches what merchants now see.

Related docs

  • Estimated prices in local currencies
  • Shopify App Pricing

title: Introducing theme app add-ons: Build and bundle apps with your themes
summary:
Theme developers can now build storefront apps using theme app extensions and bundle them with their theme listings on the Theme Store. Theme app add-ons extend your theme with advanced functionality while creating new monetization opportunities through Shopify App Pricing.

Use theme app extensions to build app blocks that integrate natively with your theme, such as:

  • Product customization and configuration tools
  • Subscription and recurring purchase management
  • Advanced product filtering, search, and wishlists

Once your storefront app is published, you can add it to your theme in the Partner Dashboard. Merchants see app add-ons featured on your theme listing page, including pricing information, featured media, app name, and subtitle. When they install your theme, they can also install your app in a single flow.

Guidelines

  • Apps must be published before added to a theme listing
  • Apps can be listed or unlisted
  • The partner organization of the theme listing must own the app
  • One app add-on per theme; unlimited reuse across multiple themes

Priority App Review

Theme developers building app add-ons will get priority in the app review queue, otherwise the usual review requirements still apply.

Resources

Learn more about building with theme app extensions and bundling apps with themes on shopify.dev.

title: Make your app's activity reportable in Shopify Analytics with App Events
summary:
You can now make your app’s activity available for merchants in Shopify Analytics. Merchants can explore your app’s metrics and dimensions in the report builder or query them with ShopifyQL using FROM app_events.

What changed

Apps can now declare events in an analytics_app_events extension. When an app sends a declared event through the App Events API, merchants can report on it in Shopify Analytics.

  • Use Shopify-defined standard events for common event types, such as emails sent.
  • Define custom events with attributes and metrics specific to your app.
  • Extend standard events with your own attributes and metrics.

Who's affected

This capability is available to developers who want merchants to report on activity from their installed apps in Shopify Analytics.

If your app already sends events for Dev Dashboard logs or billing, those events don’t automatically become available in Shopify Analytics. They must match a released Analytics App Events declaration. Existing App Events integrations don't need to change unless you want your events to appear in Shopify Analytics.

Why this matters

Merchants can now see your app's activity in Shopify Analytics, without leaving Shopify or opening a separate dashboard, and you don't need to build or host your own analytics. Your app shows up wherever merchants analyze their business.

What to do

No action is required unless you want to make app activity available in Shopify Analytics.

To get started, declare your standard or custom events in an analytics_app_events extension in shopify.extension.toml. For example, an email marketing app can declare the standard email-sent event: 

[[extensions]]
type = "analytics_app_events"
handle = "app-events"

[[extensions.events]]
name = "shopify.marketing.email_sent"
kind = "standard"

Release the configuration with shopify app deploy, then send matching events through the App Events API for stores where your app is installed.

Once the events are processed, merchants can report on emails sent over time using ShopifyQL:

FROM app_events
  SHOW emails_sent
  TIMESERIES day

Follow the App Events in Analytics guide to get started.

Related docs

  • App Events in Analytics
  • Configure Analytics App Events
  • Standard event registry
  • App Events API reference

title: App Events: Send events from Checkout and Customer Account UI extensions
summary:
Starting with API version 2027-01, Checkout and Customer Account UI extensions can send App Events to Shopify with shopify.appEvents.emit(). Extensions don't need network access or an app backend to send events. This is a new, optional API, so no action is required.

What changed

The new shopify.appEvents.emit() method sends a custom event with an event handle and optional attributes. Shopify adds your app and the shop to each event, so you don't need an access token or a shop ID. Events appear in your Dev Dashboard logs, together with the events that your app sends with the App Events API. For parameters, return values, and rate limits, refer to the API reference for Checkout UI extensions and Customer Account UI extensions.

Your extensions can also send the standard events that you declared for Shopify Analytics. Merchants see these events in their analytics.

Checkout and Customer Account send events only after the buyer allows analytics processing. Until then, events are held on the page. If the buyer declines or leaves the page, then the held events aren't sent.

Each extension can send a burst of 20 events, and then 2 events per second. When emit() doesn't send an event, it returns {success: false, error}. For example, this happens when the event is invalid or the extension exceeds the rate limit. Don't include personal information in event attributes.

Events from UI extensions aren't processed for billing. To report usage for Shopify App Pricing, continue to send billing events from your app's backend.

Who's affected

This change applies to Checkout UI extensions and Customer Account UI extensions that use API version 2027-01 or later. Extensions on earlier API versions don't have shopify.appEvents.

The server App Events API doesn't change, and apps without these extensions aren't affected. Checkouts in the Shop app don't send events from extensions.

Why this matters

Before this change, an extension needed network access and an app backend to send app events. Now an extension can send events directly, so you can see how buyers use your extension next to the rest of your app activity.

What to do

No action is required. To send events from an extension, follow these steps:

  1. Set api_version to 2027-01 in your extension's shopify.extension.toml file.
  2. Call shopify.appEvents.emit() where the event happens in your extension.
  3. In a development store, add the extension to checkout or customer account pages.
  4. If necessary, allow analytics processing as a buyer and make a test purchase. Confirm that the event appears in your Dev Dashboard logs. If you sent a declared standard event, then you can also find it in Analytics in your development store's Shopify admin.
shopify.appEvents.emit("offer_viewed", {
  offer_id: "summer_bundle",
  placement: "order_summary",
});

Related docs

  • About App Events
  • Send events from Checkout UI extensions
  • Send events from Customer Account UI extensions

title: Shopify Flow: manage automations through AI Toolkit
summary:
You can now use an external agent to manage your Shopify Flow workflows through AI Toolkit. This release is for managing your own store's workflows via AI toolkit; third-party apps are prevented from using the underlying APIs directly.

What you can do:

Through AI Toolkit, you can ask your agent to manage automations in your shop:

  • Create, update, and delete workflows.
  • Activate and deactivate workflows.
  • Get a single or list of workflows.
  • Parse a .flow file into JSON that can be used with the API.
  • Get automation tasks and environment paths in order to build the workflow.

How to get started

You can use AI toolkit or the CLI to manage your automations. Using the new APIs directly require the write_automations scope, which is a Shopify approval scope and must be approved by Shopify.

AI toolkit

If you haven't previously used AI toolkit you should first get it working with your agent of choice.

If you previously used AI toolkit, the skill may be already available to you. If not you can ask your agent to update the shopify skill: 

Install or update the shopify skill from Shopify AI toolkit so that I can manage Flow automations

CLI

You can use the shopify store execute command to call the API directly.

API

To use the automation APIs directly, you must request the write_automations in a Shopify app. This scope must be approved by Shopify.

  • Shopify Flow developer reference
  • Shopify Flow automation APIs

title: Managed mode for Shopify Tax
summary:
Shopify Tax managed mode helps Shopify apply the correct tax behavior for US sales by managing some store settings and API behavior directly. To keep those settings consistent, some Admin API writes now validate against the requirements of managed mode.

Managed mode sets requirements that Shopify uses to keep tax behavior consistent across a store. In some cases, the API now prevents apps from writing settings that would conflict with those requirements. In other cases, tax behavior now depends on more specific product or store data instead of simple boolean settings.

For app developers, the main pattern is:

  • Requests that already use the required settings, or that omit settings the app doesn't need to manage, continue to work.
  • Requests that try to override managed-mode requirements might now return validation errors.

These changes affect apps that configure markets, publish products, create custom line items, or preview checkout branding for stores that use Shopify Tax managed mode. The changes fall into four categories:

  • Breaking changes: Markets API writes and product publishing writes can now fail when they conflict with Shopify Tax managed mode requirements.

title: First sign-ins to customer accounts now set Customer.state and send customers/enable webhooks
summary:
A customer's first sign-in to customer accounts now sets Customer.state to ENABLED and sends the customers/enable and customers/update webhooks. This matches how account activation works in legacy customer accounts.

What's changing

When a customer signs in to customer accounts for the first time, Shopify sets Customer.state to ENABLED. Shopify then sends the customers/enable and customers/update webhooks. This happens for every sign-in method, including email code, Shop, Google, Facebook, Apple, and third-party identity providers.

Until now, customers who used customer accounts stayed DISABLED after they signed in. As a result, Liquid customer.has_account returned false for them. It now returns true after their first sign-in.

Customers who already signed in

Customers who signed in to customer accounts between May 27, 2024 and today are already ENABLED. Shopify set their state in a one-time update that didn't send any webhooks. Don't rely on updated_at to find these customers, because the update didn't change it for all of them. Query Customer.state instead.

Customers who haven't signed in since May 27, 2024 stay DISABLED. Their next sign-in counts as a first sign-in. It sets their state to ENABLED and sends both webhooks.

Who's affected

You're affected if your app, integration, or theme does any of the following:

  • Reads Customer.state from the GraphQL Admin API
  • Listens for the customers/enable or customers/update webhooks
  • Consumes customer.state events from the Events API
  • Uses Liquid customer.has_account to check whether a customer has an account

What you should do

Most apps don't need changes. If your app sends welcome messages, awards loyalty points, or syncs records when it receives customers/enable or sees state: ENABLED, check these things:

  • A customer's first sign-in is the moment you want your app to act.
  • Your app handles customers who became ENABLED in the one-time update. They didn't trigger webhooks, so an app that only listens for webhooks won't see them.
  • Your theme still works as you expect now that customer.has_account returns true for customers who signed in to customer accounts.

title: Add selling plans to draft order line items with the Admin GraphQL API
summary:
Admin GraphQL API version 2027-01 adds selling plan support to draft orders. You can now apply a selling plan to a draft order line item and read back the applied plan. These fields are additive, so no action is required to keep your app working.

What's added

On the GraphQL Admin API, three new fields let your app work with selling plans on draft orders:

  • DraftOrderLineItemInput.sellingPlanId sets the selling plan to apply when you create or update a draft order line item. This input field can apply to draftOrderCalculate, draftOrderCreate, and draftOrderUpdate. Note that you can only attach selling plans to product variant line items.
  • DraftOrderLineItem.sellingPlanApplication returns the selling plan applied to a line item on a saved draft order.
  • CalculatedDraftOrderLineItem.sellingPlanApplication returns the applied selling plan on the calculated draft order, so you can preview the result before you save.

The following example applies a selling plan to a line item and reads back the applied plan:

mutation {
  draftOrderCreate(input: {
    lineItems: [{
      variantId: "gid://shopify/ProductVariant/1",
      quantity: 1,
      sellingPlanId: "gid://shopify/SellingPlan/1"
    }]
  }) {
    draftOrder {
      lineItems(first: 1) {
        nodes {
          sellingPlanApplication { sellingPlanId name }
        }
      }
    }
    userErrors { field message }
  }
}

Behavior to account for

  • Only recurring and prepaid subscription plans are supported. Fixed-billing plans, such as pre-orders and try before you buy, aren't.
  • B2B draft orders, custom line items, and price overrides on selling plan lines aren't supported.
  • draftOrderComplete is not yet supported: calling draftOrderComplete on a draft that has a selling plan line item returns a user error and creates no order. You can send the draft order invoice to checkout via draftOrderInvoiceSend.

Learn more about this change in our product changelog and help docs.

  • CalculatedDraftOrderLineItem.sellingPlanApplication returns the applied selling plan on the calculated draft order, so you can preview the result before you save.

The following example applies a selling plan to a line item and reads back the applied plan:

mutation {
  draftOrderCreate(input: {
    lineItems: [{
      variantId: "gid://shopify/ProductVariant/1",
      quantity: 1,
      sellingPlanId: "gid://shopify/SellingPlan/1"
    }]
  }) {
    draftOrder {
      lineItems(first: 1) {
        nodes {
          sellingPlanApplication { sellingPlanId name }
        }
      }
    }
    userErrors { field message }
  }
}

Behavior to account for

  • Only recurring and prepaid subscription plans are supported. Fixed-billing plans, such as pre-orders and try before you buy, aren't.
  • B2B draft orders, custom line items, and price overrides on selling plan lines aren't supported.
  • draftOrderComplete is not yet supported: calling draftOrderComplete on a draft that has a selling plan line item returns a user error and creates no order. You can send the draft order invoice to checkout via draftOrderInvoiceSend.

Learn more about this change in our product changelog and help docs.

title: Cart and checkout permalinks now support UCP at /buy
summary:
Shopify storefronts now support the UCP dev.ucp.shopping.permalink capability starting with UCP 2026-08-25 on a new /buy route. You can use a single /buy link to add items to a cart, prefill checkout details, and take the buyer to checkout, using the same link format on any shop that supports UCP. You don’t need to change existing integrations to keep them working.

What changed

Shops now list the dev.ucp.shopping.permalink capability in their UCP discovery profile at /.well-known/ucp, and its config.endpoint points to the shop’s /buy route.

A /buy link encodes items in the path as token:quantity pairs and sets other cart and checkout fields with query parameters named by their UCP field path, such as buyer/email or discounts/codes/0.

With a /buy link, you can:

  • Add one or more items by variant ID
  • Prefill buyer details, such as email address
  • Set the buyer’s country and language
  • Apply discount codes
  • Indicate a preference for Shop Pay
  • Send the buyer to a specific page on the shop with a continue_to parameter

If a link can’t be applied, Shopify redirects the buyer to the continue_to destination when it’s present, or to the shop’s storefront instead of showing an error page.

Existing /cart permalinks keep working, although they’re now the legacy format. Shopify keeps supporting them, but new capabilities go to /buy. /buy doesn’t support selling plans, line item properties, cart notes, or cart attributes yet, so you should keep using /cart if you need those features.

What to do

Use /buy for new links, and move existing /cart links to /buy where you can. New capabilities only apply to /buy, and the same link format works on any business that supports UCP. Your /cart links keep working, so you can migrate on your own schedule. If you rely on selling plans, line item properties, cart notes, or cart attributes, keep using /cart for now.

Permalinks don’t use capability negotiation, so you don’t need to declare dev.ucp.shopping.permalink in your agent profile. To build a link, read config.endpoint from the shop’s discovery profile instead of constructing the /buy URL yourself.

Never put payment credentials or access tokens in a link, and avoid buyer personal details in links you share widely.

  • Cart and checkout permalinks
  • UCP permalink specification

title: Store and app install details in the Dev Dashboard
summary:
You can now view your organization’s installed apps, collaborator access, earnings, and app activity in one place in the Dev Dashboard.

title: Security update: Offline token dates, new security features
summary:
On October 20, we asked all app devs to secure their app, and told you we'd share more before any security change takes effect. Here's what's new, and what you need to do.

Offline access tokens

The migration timeline for offline access tokens remains the same: All public apps that call the Admin API must migrate to expiring offline access tokens by January 1, 2027. We're sharing an updated enforcement timeline if an app isn't migrated by then:

  • January 1, 2027: Delisted from the Shopify App Store and blocked from new installs. Existing installs keep working.
  • January 15, 2027: Merchants using the app see a warning in Shopify admin.
  • April 1, 2027: Admin API requests using non-expiring offline access tokens return HTTP 403.

January 1 is the migration deadline: The later dates give merchants time to prepare, and should not be treated as extra time to migrate. Custom apps, merchant-created apps and online access tokens are not affected. Follow the migration guide.

New security features

We've rolled out several new features this week to help secure your app:

  • Recover access with client credentials. If your app loses a refresh token, your backend can now request a new access token signed with your app's private key, without waiting for a merchant to reopen your app. Set up client credentials access.
  • Restrict API access to your own servers with an IP allowlist. List the IP addresses your servers use, and we'll reject Admin API requests from any other IP, even if it has a valid access token. Set up your IP allowlist.
  • Tell us which servers and sites your app uses. In the new [network_access] section of shopify.app.toml, list the servers your app's code loads from or sends requests to, wherever it runs on a store. We use that list to spot requests your app didn't make. You can also list the sites you link customers to, so those links skip the warning customers normally see before leaving the store. Declare your app's network access.
  • We now verify your identity before installing apps on development and client-transfer stores. This helps keep apps in trusted hands.
  • Use the new app security hub as your checklist. Every app security practice now has its own page in the dev docs. Point your agent at the hub to check which practices apply to your app, and run shopify app security check before every release. Go to the app security hub.

Get help

If you ever suspect a security issue with your app, notify us immediately at partner-security-reports@shopify.com. You are accountable to fix the problem and notify affected merchants, and we'll support you through it.

For general security inquiries, contact Shopify Support.

Questions about these updates? Ask in the App Security board in the developer community.

title: Migrate to expiring offline access tokens before January 1, 2027
summary:
Public apps still using non-expiring offline access tokens must migrate to use expiring offline access tokens before January 1, 2027 to remain listed in the Shopify App Store and continue accepting new installs.

This schedule applies to existing public apps previously covered by the January 1, 2027 deadline. The requirement for public apps created on or after April 1, 2026 remains in effect. Custom apps and apps created by merchants are excluded.

Follow the migration guide to update token acquisition, migrate existing installations, and validate token storage and refresh handling.

title: Secure your app with network access rules in `shopify.app.toml`
summary:
You can now declare your app's external hosts and servers in a new [network_access] section of shopify.app.toml. Normally Shopify warns customers when they navigate to a URL ouside Shopify; declaring your external hosts skips this warning, letting you remove friction for trusted journeys. Declaring servers, meanwhile, helps Shopify spot suspicious activity and protect your app.

What changed

The new network_access section has two properties:

  • allowed_navigation_hosts: The external sites your app links to from the storefront, such as your own domain. Shopify normally warns customers before sending them to a site outside the storefront. Links to these hosts skip that warning. List each host exactly as it appears in your links, up to 20.
  • allowed_sources: Up to 20 HTTPS origins that your app's code loads from or sends requests to on storefront, checkout, and Shopify admin pages. This includes your extensions, app home, and app proxy pages. We use the list to protect your app and monitor storefronts for malicious requests.

Here's an example configuration:

[network_access]
allowed_navigation_hosts = ["app.example.com"]
allowed_sources = ["https://api.app.example.com"]

Who's affected

Any app whose code links to or contacts external servers from a storefront, checkout, or the Shopify admin can use the new section.

What to do

For all apps, we strongly recommend you:

  1. Add the hosts that your app links customers to, such as your app's own site, to allowed_navigation_hosts.
  2. Add the servers that your app's code loads from or sends requests to, such as your API or CDN, to allowed_sources.
  3. Run shopify app deploy and release the new version.

For examples, see Declare your app's network access.

title: Restrict Admin API access with an IP allowlist
summary:
You can now limit Admin API access tokens by IP address. When you add your servers' IP addresses to an IP allowlist in the Dev Dashboard, Shopify rejects GraphQL Admin API and REST Admin API requests that use your app's tokens from anywhere else.

What changed

Your app's Settings page has a new IP allowlist section. Enter your servers' addresses or CIDR ranges, test them against recent traffic, and enable enforcement. Requests from outside your ranges fail with a 403 status code.

What to do

We strongly recommend using an IP allowlist if your app calls Shopify from static IP addresses. For setup instructions, see Restrict API access with an IP allowlist.

Note: Support for apps hosted on serverless platforms with dynamic IP addresses is coming soon.

title: Promoted Placements beta now includes Shop Campaigns
summary:
Promoted Placements is now in beta, and it includes Shop Campaigns. When a search_catalog result comes from a merchant running Shop Campaigns, you earn the commission that merchant funds, added to Shopify's base rate. No action is required.

What changed

Merchants running Shop Campaigns with external platforms turned on now include the Catalog API as one of those platforms. On their products, placement.commission.percentage.value returns the total rate, combining the merchant's commission and Shopify's base rate. Buyers who click a product with merchant-funded commission land in Shop (shop.com).

Who is affected

Organizations in the Promoted Placements beta that have accepted the terms and turned on Earn commission for a saved catalog. Access is invite-led, and you can join the waitlist from the docs.

What to do

No action is required, because commission comes back in the same field you already read. Keep passing your enrolled catalog.catalog_id on search_catalog and send buyers to the variant URL exactly as Shopify returns it. If you show a commission rate in your own reporting, read it from placement.commission.percentage.value, since it now varies by product.

Earning applies to search_catalog only, and only to products from Shopify merchants.

Related docs

  • Catalog API

title: Search brands that don't sell on Shopify in the Catalog API (beta)
summary:
You can now return products from brands that don't sell on Shopify when you search the beta Catalog API. Add the new sources parameter to search_catalog to include external products in the same response as products from Shopify merchants. If you omit sources, results stay limited to Shopify merchant products and you don't need to change any existing calls.

What changed

The Catalog API beta now supports a sources parameter on search_catalog that controls which products you return:

  • Shopify merchant products only: omit sources, or set ["shopify"]
  • Both Shopify merchant and external products: ["shopify", "external"]
  • Brands that don't sell on Shopify only: ["external"]

The sources parameter works on the existing search_catalog method, with no new endpoint to call. The get_product method returns an external product when you pass its ID, and lookup_catalog support is coming later.

External products always return eligible.native_checkout: false, so shoppers can't buy them through Shopify checkout and these products don't earn Promoted Placements commission. Each external product includes a description, an image, a price, and a link to the brand's product page so the shopper completes the purchase on the brand's own site.

Who’s affected

This change affects apps that use the Catalog API to power on-site search or recommendations and want to include products from brands that don't sell on Shopify.

During the beta, external product data comes from each brand's website, and external products only return when the shopper is in the United States. Searches for shoppers in other countries continue to return Shopify merchant products only.

What to do

No action is required if you only want to keep returning products from Shopify merchants. Your existing search_catalog calls work without changes.

If you want to include external products, update your search_catalog requests to set the sources parameter to ["shopify", "external"], or to ["external"] if you only want brands that don't sell on Shopify. If you surface links to product detail pages, make sure you handle external product URLs correctly so shoppers land on the brand’s own site when they select an external product.

Related docs

  • Learn how to return products from brands that don't sell on Shopify in the Catalog API: https://shopify.dev/docs/agents/catalog/global-catalog-extension#catalog-sources
  • Read more about Global Catalog MCP tools: https://shopify.dev/docs/agents/catalog/global-catalog

title: Analytics queryable capability is configurable in shopify.app.toml for metaobject definitions
summary:
Apps can now set capabilities.analytics_queryable on metaobject definitions in shopify.app.toml. This makes compatible fields on those definitions queryable in Shopify analytics and ShopifyQL. It applies to apps that declare metaobject definitions in their app configuration. No action is required, because the capability stays off unless you add the key.

What changed

Metaobject definitions declared under [metaobjects.app.] in shopify.app.toml now accept capabilities.analytics_queryable. When you set it to true, any field on the definition with an analytics-compatible type, such as single_line_text_field, number_integer, date, or product_reference, becomes available as a dimension and filter in analytics reports and ShopifyQL. This works wherever a product, product variant, customer, or order metafield references the metaobject. Fields with other types are ignored.

title: Unlink a customer's identity provider subject with the GraphQL Admin API
summary:
As of API version 2027-01, you can use the identityProviderSubjectDelete mutation to unlink a customer from a third-party identity provider.

Pass the customer's ID as customerId and the identity provider subject's ID as id. You can get subject IDs from Customer.identityProviderSubjects. Unlinking signs the customer out of all of their existing sessions. The next time they sign in through the identity provider, they're linked again.

The mutation requires the write_customers access scope.

title: Discover a merchant's retail stores with UCP location search and lookup
summary:
Shopify storefronts now support the UCP location capability, dev.ucp.common.location.search and dev.ucp.common.location.lookup, starting with UCP 2026-08-25. When you negotiate these capabilities over the storefront MCP endpoint, your agent can find a merchant's physical stores, narrow them by name, city, or distance, and check which stores carry the items a buyer wants. This is an optional new capability and doesn't require changes if you don't use locations today.

What changed

Storefronts with at least one retail location now list both location capabilities in their discovery profiles at /.well-known/ucp. A retail location is an active, merchant-managed location that the merchant set up to sell in person and enabled as a Physical storefront.

If your agent profile negotiates these capabilities, the storefront MCP endpoint at https://{storedomain}/api/ucp/mcp exposes two tools:

  • search_locations lists the shop's retail locations. An empty location object returns the first page. You can narrow results with a query that matches store names and cities, a distance relation with an explicit center and a max radius in meters, and filters.items.
  • lookup_locations returns locations by ID, such as gid://shopify/Location/123. It processes the first 10 distinct IDs. If you send more, the response includes a batch_limit_applied message, and you can send the rest in another request.

Each location includes its id, name, address, and geo coordinates when the merchant has set them. Search returns 10 locations by default, and up to 250 when you set pagination.limit. To get the next page, pass the pagination.cursor from the response.

filters.items accepts up to 10 product variant IDs. A location matches only when every variant is available there. Availability follows Shopify's existing store availability rules. It isn't a stock count, a pickup promise, or a reservation.

Shopify doesn't support the hours and amenities filters, custom filters, or the serves relation. Requests that include them return an invalid_input error instead of ignoring them. Pickup checkout for a selected location isn't supported.

How to set it up

Platforms and agents that use Shopify's storefront MCP endpoint with UCP 2026-08-25 and negotiate either location capability are affected.

Shops without a retail location don't advertise these capabilities or tools. Integrations that don't declare them, or that negotiate an earlier UCP version, aren't affected.

What to do

  1. Declare dev.ucp.common.location.search and dev.ucp.common.location.lookup at version 2026-08-25 in your agent profile.
  2. Call the location tools only when the shop's profile lists them.
  3. Send distance.center only from a location that the buyer chose to share. Shopify never infers a center from context or IP address.
  4. Treat item matches as provisional. Confirm availability and fulfillment options in cart and checkout before you tell the buyer that an item is ready.

Related docs

  • Configure agent profiles and UCP negotiation
  • Review the UCP location specification

title: POS UI extensions now support reactive storage access
summary:
The new shopify.storage.current API lets POS UI extension developers respond automatically when stored values change across extension targets on the same POS device. It’s now available in API version 2026-10. No changes are required for existing extensions.

What changed

shopify.storage.current exposes each storage key as a read-only reactive signal. You can read its current value or subscribe to changes made by other targets of the same extension on the same POS device. Writes and removals still use the existing Storage API methods.

For example, a background target can fetch and store a customer’s loyalty points, and a smart grid tile can react to those changes automatically. This keeps the displayed balance up to date without repeated storage reads or custom polling logic.

Stored values load asynchronously, so a signal’s value is initially undefined until its key finishes loading. Make sure you handle this initial state as well as missing keys.

Who’s affected

This addition is available to POS UI extensions that use API version 2026-10 or later. Extensions that use earlier API versions can’t use shopify.storage.current.

What to do

You don’t need to take action. Existing Storage API methods continue to work as before.

To adopt reactive storage, update your extension to use API version 2026-10 or later and read or subscribe to the keys your extension needs through shopify.storage.current.

Related docs

  • POS UI extensions Storage API reference

title: POS UI extensions 2026-10 adds s-pos-list, a virtualized list with custom row templates
summary:
POS UI extensions API version 2026-10 adds s-pos-list, a virtualized list component for Polaris web components. You pass rows as plain data and lay out each kind of row with a template built from web components. s-pos-list is now available in Shopify POS 11.17.0 and later, and it replaces the List component from API version 2025-07 and earlier for extensions that adopt 2026-10. No action is required.

What changed

The List component ended with API version 2025-07, and Polaris web components had no list component to replace it. s-pos-list fills that gap. Instead of List’s fixed row layout, each kind of row gets its own template, so one list can mix headings, dividers, and content rows.

Who's affected

Extensions that set api_version = "2026-10" and run on Shopify POS 11.17.0 or later can use s-pos-list. API version 2026-07 and earlier don’t include it, and nothing changes for extensions that stay on earlier API versions or keep using List.

It’s for extensions that used List and are moving to Polaris web components, and for extensions that build long lists by mapping rows into s-scroll-box.

Why this matters

Mapping rows into s-scroll-box makes POS create a view for every row, so display time and memory grow with the list, and very large lists can fail to display. s-pos-list recycles row views as the POS user scrolls. In testing on an iPad (A16) with the most complex List row layout, s-pos-list displays and scrolls large lists as fast as the 2025-07 List.

What to do

You don’t need to change existing extensions, because s-pos-list is a new component and existing extensions keep working unchanged. When you adopt API version 2026-10 and run on Shopify POS 11.17.0 or later, you can use the following mappings to move List implementations to s-pos-list:

| List (2025-07) | s-pos-list (2026-10) | |

title: Metaobject analytics queryable capability available in the Admin API
summary:
Starting with GraphQL Admin API version 2027-01, you can read and configure the analyticsQueryable capability on metaobject definitions. This applies to apps that create, update, or inspect metaobject definitions. No action is required unless you want your app to control whether a metaobject definition can be queried in analytics.

What changed

The GraphQL Admin API now exposes the analytics queryable capability for metaobject definitions.

You can read MetaobjectCapabilities.analyticsQueryable, which includes:

  • eligible: whether the metaobject definition can use the capability. A definition is eligible if at least one of its fields uses an analytics-compatible type.
  • enabled: whether the capability is currently enabled.

You can also set the capability when you create or update a metaobject definition by using:

  • MetaobjectCapabilityCreateInput.analyticsQueryable
  • MetaobjectCapabilityUpdateInput.analyticsQueryable
  • MetaobjectCapabilityAnalyticsQueryableInput.enabled

The MetaobjectCapabilityType enum now includes ANALYTICS_QUERYABLE, and MetaobjectUserErrorCode includes CAPABILITY_NOT_ELIGIBLE for definitions that can’t enable the capability.

Who's affected

This change applies to apps that use GraphQL Admin API version 2027-01 or later to create, update, or inspect metaobject definitions.

Apps that use earlier versions don’t see the analyticsQueryable field, input, enum value, or error code. Existing apps don’t need to make changes unless they want to support analytics queryability for metaobject definitions.

Why this matters

You can now determine whether a metaobject definition is eligible to be queried in analytics and enable that capability through the public GraphQL Admin API. This brings metaobject definitions in line with metafield definitions, and you get consistent control over which custom data types appear in analytics.

What to do

No action is required.

If you want to use this capability:

  1. Update your app to use GraphQL Admin API version 2027-01 or later.
  2. Update your metaobject definition queries or mutations to include analyticsQueryable.

For example, to read a metaobject definition’s capabilities, include:

capabilities {
  analyticsQueryable {
    eligible
    enabled
  }
}

When you create or update a metaobject definition, set analyticsQueryable.enabled in the capability input. Check eligible first, and handle CAPABILITY_NOT_ELIGIBLE in mutation user errors. Use this method to confirm whether a definition supports the capability and give clear feedback when it doesn't.

Related docs

  • GraphQL Admin API reference
  • Metaobjects in Shopify apps

title: Securing your app, together
summary:
Merchants install your app because they trust it, and because they trust the Shopify App Store. There are bad actors out there who are motivated to exploit that trust. Alongside the rest of the industry, we are seeing the number of attacks increasing across the app ecosystem as AI gets better at finding vulnerabilities.

Security is the most important thing you can work on right now. We’re asking every app developer to act on the steps below this week.

  • Scan your app with our new security check. A single prompt with AI Toolkit checks for Shopify-specific vulnerabilities, such as unauthenticated routes, cross-shop data access and unverified webhooks. In early access, most partners found something they didn’t know about.
  • Move to expiring access tokens. Short-lived tokens limit the damage if a token leaks. This will soon be required for all public apps, so start your migration now.
  • Use vulnerability scanners to ensure all endpoints of your app are secured.
  • Treat all rendered data, whether pulled from metafields or your own servers, as untrusted, ensuring inputs are thoroughly escaped and sanitized.
  • Check your Dev Dashboard to look at your API requests and ensure you do not see any suspicious activity. To get started, filter your logs by client IP to look at traffic patterns and find suspicious sources.
  • Protect every account that touches your app. Turn on two-step authentication for your Partner account, hosting, CDN, code repositories and email. Remove access for anyone who no longer needs it.
  • Keep your emergency contact current. Make sure your emergency developer email in the Partner Dashboard reaches someone who can act quickly.
  • Review and apply the security best practices in Shopify Dev Docs.

What we’re doing alongside you

We’re tightening the boundaries for storefront app code, adding IP address restrictions so your keys only work from your servers, and raising App Store security requirements. We’ll share details and timelines with you before any change takes effect, so you have time to prepare. We’ll keep investing in platform protections, developer tools and guidance that make secure development the default.

If you ever suspect a security issue with your app, notify us immediately at partner-security-reports@shopify.com. You are accountable to fix the problem and notify affected merchants, and we’ll support you through it.

For general security inquiries, contact Shopify Support.
